blocks.text: A blacksmith in Kano hammers a copper rod flat without shattering it, then draws it into wire. Try that with a lump of salt and it turns to powder. Both are crystalline solids. The difference lies in what happens when their layers are pushed past one another.

blocks.title: Metallic bond
blocks.text: A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a regular lattice of positive metal ions and the sea of delocalised electrons that surrounds them. The outer electrons no longer belong to any individual atom and are free to move throughout the whole structure.

blocks.markdown:
## Metallic properties explained

Every physical property of a metal follows from that picture.

- **Electrical conductivity** — the delocalised electrons drift towards the positive terminal, carrying charge. No ions need to move, so a solid metal conducts.
- **Thermal conductivity** — mobile electrons carry kinetic energy quickly from the hot end to the cold end.
- **Malleability and ductility** — when layers of ions slide over one another the electron sea simply flows with them, so the bonding is maintained and the metal changes shape without breaking.
- **High melting point and density** — the ions are closely packed and strongly attracted to the electron sea.
- **Lustre** — the free electrons reflect light.

Strength of metallic bonding rises with the charge on the ion and falls with ionic size, which is why magnesium (Mg2+) melts far higher than sodium (Na+).

blocks.title: Why ionic solids are brittle but metals are not
blocks.text: Displacing one layer in an ionic lattice brings ions of the same charge opposite each other. The sudden repulsion splits the crystal. In a metal every layer is surrounded by the same electron sea, so displacement changes nothing and the metal simply bends.

blocks.markdown:
## Forces between molecules

Inside a molecule, atoms are held by strong covalent bonds. Between separate molecules there are much weaker attractions called **intermolecular forces**. These are what you overcome when a molecular substance melts or boils.

1. **Van der Waals forces (dispersion forces)** — present in all molecules. They arise from momentary uneven distribution of electrons and grow stronger as the molecule gets bigger. This is why boiling point rises down the alkane series and down group VII.
2. **Dipole-dipole attraction** — between permanently polar molecules such as HCl.
3. **Hydrogen bonding** — the strongest of the three. It occurs when hydrogen is bonded directly to the small, highly electronegative atoms fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen.

blocks.title: Why water boils so much higher than hydrogen sulphide
blocks.prompt: H2O has a relative molecular mass of 18 and boils at 100 degrees Celsius. H2S has a relative molecular mass of 34 and boils at -60 degrees Celsius. Explain this apparent contradiction.

steps.text: On molecular mass alone H2S should boil higher, because heavier molecules normally have stronger van der Waals forces.
In water, hydrogen is bonded to oxygen, which is small and very electronegative. The O-H bond is therefore strongly polar and the hydrogen carries a substantial partial positive charge.
That hydrogen is attracted to a lone pair on the oxygen of a neighbouring molecule, forming a hydrogen bond. Each water molecule can form up to four such bonds.
Sulphur is much larger and considerably less electronegative than oxygen, so the S-H bond is only weakly polar and no hydrogen bonding occurs in H2S.
Boiling water requires enough energy to break an extensive network of hydrogen bonds, while boiling H2S only requires overcoming weak van der Waals forces.

blocks.answer: Water boils far higher because extensive hydrogen bonding between its molecules must be overcome, whereas H2S has only weak van der Waals forces.

items: Water has an unusually high boiling point and high specific heat capacity
Ice is less dense than liquid water, because hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice, so ice floats
Water is an excellent solvent for ionic and polar substances
Ammonia and hydrogen fluoride also boil higher than their group neighbours for the same reason

blocks.title: Name the force before you compare
blocks.text: When asked to compare boiling points, first state which intermolecular force each substance has, then compare their strengths. Answers that jump straight to 'A boils higher than B' without naming hydrogen bonding or van der Waals forces rarely score full marks.

points: Metallic bonding is the attraction between positive ions and a sea of delocalised electrons.
Delocalised electrons explain conductivity, and sliding layers explain malleability and ductility.
Intermolecular forces are much weaker than the covalent bonds within molecules.
Van der Waals forces exist between all molecules and strengthen as molecules get larger.
Hydrogen bonding occurs when hydrogen is attached to fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen, and it explains the anomalous properties of water.
